questions.q: « Je ne dis jamais rien à personne. » What does it mean?
choices: I never say anything to anyone
I sometimes say something to someone
I always tell everyone everything
I don't say nothing to nobody, so I do talk
questions.why: French stacks negative words freely and they do not cancel out. There is only ever one ne, and the fixed order is plus, jamais, then rien or personne.

choices: Je n'ai rien.
Je n'ai pas rien.
Je n'ai plus rien.
Je n'ai pas encore mangé.
questions.why: Pas cannot combine with rien, personne, jamais, plus or aucun. The single exception is pas encore, which behaves as one unit.

questions.q: Build the sentence: There's never anyone here any more.
questions.why: The order of the negative elements is fixed: plus, then jamais, then rien or personne.

questions.q: Which is correct for « He only eats vegetables » ?
choices: Il ne mange que de légumes.
Il ne mange que des légumes.
Il ne mange pas que des légumes.
Il ne mange rien que des légumes.
questions.why: Ne … que looks negative but is not, so the article survives: que des légumes. A real negation would collapse des to de.

questions.q: He doesn't only eat vegetables: « Il ne mange ___ que des légumes. »
questions.why: Pas que is the one place pas teams up with que, and together they mean not only.

questions.q: What is the difference between « Je ne bois que du thé le matin » and « Je ne bois du thé que le matin » ?
choices: There is none, que can move freely
The first says tea is all I drink in the morning; the second says morning is the only time I drink tea
The first says morning is the only time I drink tea; the second says tea is all I drink
The second is ungrammatical
questions.why: Que restricts whatever immediately follows it, so moving it moves the meaning.

questions.q: Say « Je n'ai que dix euros » with an ordinary adverb instead: « J'ai ___ dix euros. »
questions.why: Seulement carries the same meaning with no ne at all. The other alternative is ne faire que: il ne fait que se plaindre.

questions.q: What does « J'ai peur qu'il ne vienne » mean?
choices: I'm afraid he won't come
I'm afraid he will come
I'm not afraid he'll come
I'm afraid he might not have come
questions.why: This is the ne explétif: it carries no negative meaning after avoir peur que, avant que, à moins que or a comparative. Only adding pas would negate it.

questions.q: Il est parti sans ___ dire. (without saying anything)
questions.why: Sans is already negative, so it takes no ne and no pas, and the words that follow it are rien and personne, never quelque chose or quelqu'un.

questions.q: Which is correct for « I drink neither tea nor coffee » ?
choices: Je ne bois ni du thé ni du café.
Je ne bois ni thé ni café.
Je bois ni thé ni café.
Je ne bois pas ni thé ni café.
questions.why: Ni … ni deletes indefinite and partitive articles entirely. The definite article does survive when the noun is specific: je n'aime ni le thé ni le café.
Even when ni … ni is the subject, ne still stands in front of the verb, and the verb is usually plural.

questions.q: Type what you hear, in full written French.
questions.why: In speech this comes out as c'est pas grave. The negation survives because pas survives: in fast French, pas is the syllable to listen for.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I'd rather not go (there).
questions.why: When you negate an infinitive, both halves stay together in front of it, along with any pronoun. Compare the sign: Ne pas fumer.

questions.q: Say this out loud: without ever complaining.
questions.why: Sans supplies the negation on its own, so jamais joins it directly with no ne and no pas.

questions.q: Explain what the ne explétif is, name three triggers, and say how you tell it apart from a real negation.
a: It is a ne that carries no negative meaning, used in formal French after avoir peur que / craindre que, avant que, à moins que, de peur que, empêcher que, and after a comparative. You tell it apart by looking for pas: only pas makes the clause negative. J'ai peur qu'il ne vienne means I'm afraid he will come; j'ai peur qu'il ne vienne pas means I'm afraid he won't. It is optional and increasingly rare — recognise it, you never need to write it.
questions.why: Misreading an expletive ne reverses the meaning of the whole sentence, which is why it is worth recognising on sight.
